source.title: Trust Functions: Near-Lossless Weak-to-Strong Generalization by Learning When to Trust the Weak Teacher
source.authors: Arda Uzunouglu; Alvin Zhang; Daniel Khashabi

page_placements.theme: Weak-label fine-tuning leaves the strong student below its own pre-fine-tuning performance or erodes its representations

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains stronger students on weak-teacher labels and reports student performance and recovery relative to ground-truth training. Its main intervention filters the weakly labelled data using learned trust scores, and its recovery measure is not Burns et al.'s PGR.
record.gate_note: Rows below record the paper's domain-averaged or task-averaged student-training results, including the Naive weak-label baseline. Parenthetical percentages are the paper's recovery measure, defined relative to the no-training baseline and ground-truth training, not PGR relative to the weak teacher. Other selection methods are compared in the same tables; they are not all included as separate rows. NTF trust-prediction metrics and representation ablations are not weak-to-strong student-performance results.
record.test_reason: The study trains larger students on smaller-teacher labels in three domains (MCQA, GRPO on math, chess). It reports teacher, naive weak-label, filtered weak-label and budget-matched ground-truth accuracies, so PGR can be computed from its tables even though it reports a different 'recovery' measure. Its main method is trust-based filtering of weak labels, compared against naive training, which bears on V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors frame weak-to-strong as a data-selection problem. They conclude that trust-filtered weak supervision often matches and sometimes beats budget-matched ground-truth training (near-lossless or super-recovery). They find that chaining compounds gains, and that the benefits come from an easy-first selection bias, recovering strong alternative chess moves, and more coherent gradients.
record.recipe_differences: Like weak-to-strong fine-tuning, the study trains stronger students using weaker-model labels. It adds a learned trust-function filter before training and reports recovery relative to no-training and ground-truth baselines, not Burns et al.'s PGR. The domain training recipes include LoRA-SFT and GRPO.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by domain, teacher/student model family and scale, and training budget. Trust-function transfer is strong for in-domain distribution shifts but weak across task interfaces; trust prediction also varies with layer, token position, pooling, and training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: Naive weak-label training can push a strong student below its own untrained baseline while staying above the teacher. Example: OpenBookQA OLMo2-13B Naive 54.2 vs No-SFT 65.4 (Table 26).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-label fine-tuning can degrade a strong student's pre-existing capability, even when it still beats the teacher.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study does not calculate PGR, so its recovery percentages are not directly comparable to the claim's measure. Several displayed results are averages across benchmarks, and row-specific uncertainty is not given for most table entries. Chess results report means over 5 runs. The authors also note that the risk-control threshold's main-text bound omits a multiple-testing correction; the corrected procedure is too conservative in their setting.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the many alternative selector rows (I-Confidence, ICL + I-Confidence, verbalized confidence, ensemble, reward models) in Tables 2–4 and per-benchmark breakdowns in Tables 24–28, to prioritize NTF and Naive results across the model/task conditions. Also left out Table 12's student-training-budget sweep and the trust-function accuracy/calibration and representation ablations in Tables 1, 8–16; these do not report the primary weak-to-strong comparison used here. Table 17's Gemma3-1B-to-Llama3.1-8B transfer is not included in the 60-row selection; it reports 51.08 for NTF, 92.2% recovery, and 51.72 for ground truth.

untested.parts: Auxiliary confidence loss and loss variants are not tested. Ensembling is tested only as two-teacher agreement selection, which no row records.
No reward-modelling task and no analysis of what predicts PGR. The paper reports its own no-training-based recovery rather than PGR.

Not tested: exploitation of what the weak supervisor can't check, PGR under distribution shift, and correlated weak/strong errors. Distribution-shift results concern trust-function AUC, not student PGR.

missing.what: Gemma3-1B-it→Llama3.1-8B-Instruct MATH results: teacher 43.52, No-GRPO 45.76, Naive 42.96, I-Conf 41.32, V-Conf 44.24, NTF 51.08, GT 51.72. Naive is below the teacher, so PGR is below 0.
Ensemble (two-teacher agreement) and I-Confidence selection vs Naive across MCQA pairs
Naive Chain and Naive/NTF Shallow comparators for the bootstrapping chain

record.verdict_notes: Recovery in the paper is (method − untrained student)/(GT − untrained student), not PGR. PGR was computed here from the reported teacher, method and GT accuracies. In MCQA and math the untrained student already exceeds the teacher (e.g. OLMo2-7B No-SFT 65.1 vs teacher 43.1), so V1's 'beats supervisor' is near-trivial there; chess (student baseline 0) is the informative V1 setting. GT is a budget-matched subset, not a full ceiling. Ten rows are same-model self-training and were unlinked. The record's V3 limits_scope label was folded into the V3 supports label, because family/task variation is what V3 describes.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports student scores and teacher performance, but does not calculate Burns et al.'s PGR or use its exact formula.
Tests trust-based data filtering against naive selection and other selection baselines, but not auxiliary confidence losses or loss variants.
Varies task/domain and teacher/student scales, and analyzes selection and gradient mechanisms. Does not report PGR by size/task, reward-modelling results, or a predictive analysis of PGR itself.

Does not test whether students exploit what weak supervisors cannot check, whether weak-to-strong student gains fall under distribution shift, or whether gains depend on correlated weak/strong errors. It does test transfer of the trust function across data regimes, which is not this version's outcome.
No theorem establishing conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality experiment.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope

reader_labels.reason: The reported recovery is not uniformly near-lossless: OLMo2 strategy-game students recover 77.9 and 76.1, and the authors state that this family has a harder time eliminating the gap to ground truth (R26–R27).
